title: Effects of the location of sound masking loudspeakers on cognitive performance in open-plan offices: Local sound masking is as efficient as conventional sound masking
research_question: To evaluate if the location and configuration of sound masking emitters have an effect on cognitive performance and perceived annoyance when employees are subjected to disturbing background speech. Specifically: 1. Does placing sound masking emitters close to the speech source show a beneficial effect on working memory performance and annoyance as compared to a spatial separation by 90°? 2. Is local sound masking as efficient with respect to working memory performance and annoyance as compared to conventional sound masking with six spatially distributed emitters in the ceiling? 3. Does conventional sound masking with a broadband masking spectrum that begins at 100 Hz improve working memory performance and reduce annoyance as compared to a masking spectrum that begins at 200 Hz? 4. Does sound masking at -9 and -12 dB SNR increase working memory performance and reduce annoyance perception as compared to unmasked speech?

participants.description: 25 employees (6 female) aged 21 to 64 years (median = 38, standard deviation = 13.9), native German speakers, reported normal hearing.
participants.recruitment: Employees of the organization where the study was conducted.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Open-plan office environment (79 m²) with room-high sound screens, cabinets, acoustic panels, indirect lighting (800 lux), temperature 23-25 °C, relative humidity 60-70%, CO2 500-850 ppm. Room acoustic parameters: VD,1 = 3 m, VD,2 = 5 m, VP,1 = 7m, rp,2 = 11 m, D2,S,1 = 14 dB, D2,S,2 = 16 dB, Lp,A,S,4m,1 = 28 dB(A), Lp,A,S,4m,2 = 38 dB(A).

Twelve different sound conditions: silence (REF0), unmasked speech (T1_0), and ten masked speech conditions. Masked conditions varied by speech source location (T1 lateral, T2 behind), masker location (M1 local lateral, M2 local behind, M0 ceiling), SNR (-9 dB, -12 dB), and masker HPF cutoff (200 Hz, 100 Hz). Speech signals were dry recordings of German sentences (Hochmair-Schulz-Moser test) played at 33 or 36 dB(A). Masking sound was filtered pink noise (5 dB/octave decline) played at 45 dB(A).

measures.instrument: Serial recall task (percentage of incorrectly recalled digit positions)
Five-point Likert scale and eleven-point numerical scale (0-10) according to ISO/TS 15666:2003

findings.antecedent: Sound condition
findings.consequent: Mean error rate in serial recall task
findings.mechanism: Different sound conditions have a significant impact on cognitive performance.
findings.quote: A repeated measures analysis of variance revealed a significant main effect of sound condition on the mean error rate in the serial recall task (F(11,253) = 3.48, mean squared error = 0.0074, p < 0.001, η² = 0.13).

findings.antecedent: Sound condition
findings.mechanism: Different sound conditions have a significant impact on perceived annoyance.
findings.quote: A repeated measures analysis of variance showed a significant main effect of sound condition on the perceived annoyance (F(11,220) = 34.4, mean squared error = 0.44, p < 0.001, η² = 0.63).

findings.antecedent: Masked speech from T1 with local M2 masker at -9 dB SNR (T1M2_9)
findings.mechanism: Sound masking with spatial separation (90°) at -9 dB SNR does not significantly reduce annoyance compared to unmasked speech.
findings.quote: When the speech sounds were masked, the sound environment was perceived as less annoying than during unmasked speech except from the sound condition with a difference in horizontal direction of 90° at - 9 dB SNR (T1M2_9).

findings.antecedent: Masked speech from T1 with local M2 masker at -9 dB SNR (T1M2_9) vs. Masked speech from T2 with local M1 masker at -9 dB SNR (T2M1_9)
findings.mechanism: Different spatial separations (T1M2_9 vs T2M1_9) lead to different subjective perception of annoyance, but not working memory performance.
findings.quote: Different behaviour between the opposite spatial separations (T1M2_9 and T2M1_9) was only observed in subjective perception but not in working memory performance.

findings.antecedent: Masking sound with HPF 100 Hz (T1M4_9) vs. Masking sound with HPF 200 Hz (T1M3_9) at -9 dB SNR
findings.consequent: Mean error rate in serial recall task
findings.mechanism: Including the 125 Hz octave band in the masking spectrum improves cognitive performance, particularly for male speech fundamental tones.
findings.quote: at - 9 dB SNR significantly fewer errors were made when the cutoff frequency of the masking sound was 100 Hz (T1M4_9) but not when it was increased to 200 Hz (T1M3_9).

findings.antecedent: Masking sound with HPF 100 Hz (T1M4_12) vs. Masking sound with HPF 200 Hz (T1M3_12) at -12 dB SNR (compared to silent control)
findings.consequent: Mean error rate in serial recall task
findings.mechanism: The advantage of including 125 Hz octave band in masking is not significant at -12 dB SNR compared to silence, implying no significant difference between the 100 Hz and 200 Hz HPF conditions at this SNR.
findings.quote: In comparison to the silent control condition, the mean error rates at 12 dB SNR were significantly higher when the cutoff frequency of the masking sound was 200 Hz (T1M3-12) but no significant difference occurred when it was decreased to 100 Hz (T1M4-12).

findings.antecedent: Masking sound with HPF 100 Hz vs. Masking sound with HPF 200 Hz
findings.mechanism: Low frequency components (100-200 Hz) in masking sound do not significantly affect annoyance perception.
findings.quote: The subjective perception did not reveal the above-mentioned masking gain due to low frequency elements.

findings.antecedent: Spatial separation of target speech and masking sound (90° horizontal)
findings.mechanism: Spatial separation of target speech and masking sound has a negative impact on cognitive performance, as evidenced by higher error rates compared to silence in conditions like T1M2_12.
findings.quote: the paired comparisons towards both control conditions provide some evidence that spatial separation of a target speech and masking sound source has a negative impact on the resulting cognitive performance.

findings.antecedent: Masking sound from ceiling emitters (conventional M0, HPF 200 Hz) at -9 dB SNR
findings.mechanism: Conventional ceiling masking with 200 Hz HPF at -9 dB SNR does not significantly improve working memory performance compared to unmasked speech.
findings.quote: The conventional sound masking system (T1M3_9) did not result in significantly lower working memory performance as compared to unmasked speech.

findings.antecedent: Local sound masking (M1, M2) without spatial separation vs. conventional sound masking (M0)
findings.mechanism: Conventional ceiling masking results in similar annoyance ratings as local masking without spatial separation.
findings.quote: Sound masking without spatial separation and conventional sound masking resulted in similar annoyance ratings.

findings.antecedent: Local sound masking (M1, M2) vs. conventional sound masking (M0)
findings.mechanism: Local and conventional sound masking result in similar error rates regardless of whether spatial separation occurs.
findings.quote: The overall results suggest that local and conventional sound masking result in similar error rates and annoyance ratings regardless of whether spatial separation occurs.

findings.antecedent: Local sound masking (M1, M2) vs. conventional sound masking (M0)
findings.mechanism: Local and conventional sound masking result in similar annoyance ratings regardless of whether spatial separation occurs.
findings.quote: The overall results suggest that local and conventional sound masking result in similar error rates and annoyance ratings regardless of whether spatial separation occurs.

findings.antecedent: Speech and masking sound from the same direction
findings.mechanism: Presenting distracting speech and a masking sound from the same direction may have a beneficial effect on cognitive performance.
findings.quote: Presenting distracting speech and a masking sound from the same direction may even have a beneficial effect on cognitive performance.

findings.antecedent: SNR (-9 dB and -12 dB)
findings.mechanism: Appropriate SNRs (-9 and -12 dB) are sufficient to improve cognitive performance.
findings.quote: The results suggest that SNRs of -9 and -12 dB are sufficient to improve both, the cognitive performance and subjective perception of employees that perform cognitively demanding tasks in an open-plan office.

findings.antecedent: SNR (-9 dB and -12 dB)
findings.mechanism: Appropriate SNRs (-9 and -12 dB) are sufficient to improve acoustic satisfaction (reduce annoyance).
findings.quote: The results suggest that SNRs of -9 and -12 dB are sufficient to improve both, the cognitive performance and subjective perception of employees that perform cognitively demanding tasks in an open-plan office.

mechanisms: Irrelevant background speech interferes with short-term/working memory processing (interference-by-process principle, changing-state hypothesis).
Sound masking reduces temporal-spectral variability of background speech, improving working memory performance.
Spatial release from masking, which typically improves speech reception, may lead to a disadvantage in working memory performance when masker and speech are spatially separated.
The diffuseness of the masking sound field affects masking performance and acceptance.
Low frequency components (100-200 Hz) in masking sound can improve cognitive performance, possibly by masking male speech fundamental tones.

Higher annoyance of M2 (behind, 90° separation from T1) compared to M1 (lateral, same direction as T1) might be due to M2 being closer to the subject's head, making the masking sound more apparent and directional.
The perceived annoyance and cognitive performance decrease monotonically with SNR.
Presenting distracting speech and a masking sound from the same direction may have a beneficial effect on cognitive performance.
moderators: Masker location (local vs. conventional, same direction vs. 90° separation)
Masker frequency spectrum (HPF 100 Hz vs. 200 Hz)
implementation_implications: Sound masking can improve cognitive performance and acoustic satisfaction at appropriate SNRs (-9 and -12 dB).
Including the 125 Hz octave band in the sound masking spectrum may provide an advantage for cognitive performance.
Investing in sound masking emitters with an extended frequency response (down to 100 Hz) pays off.
Local and individualised sound masking that matches the direction of distracting speech may improve cognitive performance at higher SNRs than conventional systems.
Higher SPLs for local systems might be accepted over short time frames if they can be switched off.
Educating employees about sound masking functionality is important for acceptance.

limitations: The open-plan office environment, with room-high partitions, was not comparable to a conventional open-plan office, limiting generalizability.
The sound fields of speech and masking sounds may differ notably between this setup and conventional open offices.
The perceived distance of speech and masking sound sources, which depends on the direct-to-reverberant energy ratio, may impact annoyance and acoustic satisfaction.
The diffuseness of the masking sound field might have been suboptimal due to face-down ceiling emitters and room-high partitions.
The subjects did not leave the workplace while the system was switched on, potentially limiting their perception of spatial differences in the masking sound field.
The distances of the speech sources (approximately 3 and 4 m) were relatively small, which might be too short for effective sound masking if communication is desired.

The study considered only sound conditions with one disturbing background speech signal with a single voice present at a time, whereas multi-talker environments are more realistic and might yield different results for annoyance and performance.
